profiles.meeting_scenario: A brainstorming meeting at a university-affiliated interdisciplinary research cluster that is preparing a pilot initiative based on a publication network visualization tool. The cluster spans engineering, public health, economics, and materials science, and leadership has asked for a short list of low-risk ways the visualization could be used to support interdisciplinary innovation without creating unhealthy performance pressure. The agenda is to generate candidate uses for the tool, discuss how the pilot should be framed for researchers, and identify what a 'lightweight' first rollout would look like. The expected outcome is a small set of brainstormed pilot concepts and an informal shared sense of what kind of prototype and launch approach they will take to the cluster steering committee.

members.name: Dr. Lena Vogt
members.expertise: Interdisciplinary program design, faculty engagement, research evaluation framing
members.background: Lena manages collaboration initiatives for a large cross-faculty research cluster and previously worked in a national science foundation office where she designed support programs for cross-disciplinary teams.
members.private_state: She wants ideas that cluster leadership can approve quickly as a low-friction support intervention, and she is quietly worried that anything perceived as researcher ranking or surveillance will trigger resistance from senior faculty.
hidden_assumptions: A 'pilot' should feel voluntary and low-stakes, with outputs framed as exploratory support material rather than operational infrastructure.
If the tool is described as helping people find collaborators, most researchers will assume it is based on broadly visible publication data and not expect major data-governance discussion.

When people say a rollout should work at the 'team level,' they usually mean principal investigators and work-package leads can see aggregated collaboration patterns, not individual career-level profiles.
A 'useful signal' from the visualization means a conversation starter that surfaces plausible collaboration opportunities, even if it is not complete or fully standardized across disciplines.

members.name: Arjun Mehta
members.expertise: Bibliometrics, research information systems, network analytics, dashboard prototyping
members.background: Arjun leads a small analytics team in the university library's digital scholarship unit and has built internal publication dashboards and co-authorship maps for several institutes.
members.private_state: He wants the pilot to demonstrate enough technical credibility that it can later become a recurring institutional service, and he is quietly concerned that vague framing will lead to a toy demo that nobody trusts.
hidden_assumptions: A 'pilot' should be implemented on the same architecture and data pipeline that would support later institutional deployment, even if the interface is minimal.
Any visualization presented inside a research cluster should rely on cleaned, person-resolved institutional publication records rather than only public bibliographic feeds.
When stakeholders say the tool should support 'teams,' they normally expect views that can drill down from cluster structure to lab groups and named researchers so coordinators can act on them.
A 'useful signal' from the visualization means a pattern robust enough to defend methodologically across fields, including normalized comparisons and disambiguated author identities.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both agree to start with a 'lightweight pilot' before anything larger.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means a low-friction concept pilot: a manually assembled or semi-manual demo using readily available publication records for a few cluster members, mainly to test reactions and facilitation value.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means a minimally scoped but production-grade pilot: the real ingestion and cleaning pipeline, author disambiguation, and reusable dashboard backbone, just for a smaller subset of users.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: In brainstorming meetings, 'lightweight pilot' sounds like obvious shared caution and usually signals pace rather than implementation method, so neither person feels a need to unpack the operational details.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both say the first version should stay at the 'team level' to avoid pressure.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means the visualization should stop at aggregated cluster, project, or work-package patterns and avoid exposing named individuals except perhaps principal investigators already publicly associated with projects.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means the default screen can summarize teams, but users should still be able to click into member-level nodes because otherwise coordinators cannot identify actual collaboration candidates.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The phrase 'team-level' sounds reassuringly general and aligned with a non-punitive rollout, while the disagreement concerns the edge of what is included, not the stated intent.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both agree the pilot should be 'useful for finding potential collaborators.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 thinks usefulness means researchers recognize surprising but plausible cross-disciplinary links that improve conversations, even if the map is incomplete, static, or partly qualitative.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 thinks usefulness means the map produces defensible and repeatable recommendations or patterns based on normalized, cleaned data that users can trust for decision support.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Because both are positively oriented toward collaboration support, the term 'useful' masks a difference between conversational usefulness and methodological robustness, a second-order distinction rarely made explicit in early ideation.

misalignment_points.topic: Which publication data is already assumed
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both discuss building the network from 'the publication data we already have.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 assumes this means public and already visible records such as Web of Science, Scopus exports, ORCID links, and existing CV lists that can be gathered quickly for a few volunteer researchers.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 assumes this refers to the university's internal current research information system records with affiliation cleaning, identity resolution, and permissions already covered under existing institutional processes.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Each member treats the availability and legitimacy of their preferred data source as institutional background knowledge, so the phrase 'already have' feels too mundane to interrogate during a brainstorming session.

turns.inner_thought: I need something steering can approve in one pass: clearly supportive, clearly non-evaluative, and easy to explain. If this starts sounding like monitoring individual researchers, senior faculty will push back immediately. A lightweight pilot should be a low-stakes concept test, maybe even a manually assembled example for discussion. And if we keep it at the team level, people will hear that as aggregated and safe. Useful here just means it helps people notice possible interdisciplinary connections and talk differently.
turns.utterance: Thanks for making time. The cluster leadership is looking for a lightweight pilot around publication network visualization—something useful for finding potential collaborators, but framed in a way that supports interdisciplinary teams without creating pressure. My hope is that we sketch a few low-risk uses and a sensible first rollout.

turns.inner_thought: That sounds right, as long as lightweight doesn't mean throwaway. If we do this, I want the pilot to prove the approach can stand up and eventually become a service. We should build from the publication data we already have, meaning the institutional records and identity resolution we maintain, and just keep the initial scope small enough to manage.
turns.utterance: Yes, that makes sense. A lightweight pilot can still give us a solid base if we work from the publication data we already have and keep the first scope contained. That way we learn something real without overcommitting.

turns.inner_thought: A single theme is the safest way to test reactions. I want something workshop-friendly: one map, one discussion, no sense that anyone is being profiled. Team level means theme, project, or work-package patterns—not named early-career people on display. If people can quickly see proximity across areas, that's enough for a first pass.
turns.utterance: One possible use case for the first pass would be a team-level map for just one cluster theme, so members can quickly see who sits near whom intellectually and where there may be room to connect across the theme.

turns.inner_thought: Good starting point. For it to actually support action, coordinators will need to move from the team-level view into the underlying people and links; otherwise they can't make introductions. That's still consistent with starting at team level as the default. And if the patterns are methodologically sound, it becomes genuinely useful for finding potential collaborators rather than just decorative.
turns.utterance: I like that. We could make the opening view a team-level overview and then have clear drill-down paths, so coordinators can identify concrete people to introduce across labs when something interesting shows up.

turns.inner_thought: I need to steer this back toward a facilitation format before it turns into a full platform pitch. For me, useful is if the map sparks a better conversation at a retreat. It does not need live interaction or a robust backbone yet; a static visual in a workshop would be enough to test whether researchers respond well.
turns.utterance: For the pilot, I think it only needs to be useful enough to spark better conversations at the annual cluster retreats. I can easily imagine a static visual that people discuss in small workshops, just to see what kinds of connections they notice.

turns.inner_thought: Static is fine for the front end if needed, but the credibility has to come from the underlying data. If we rely on ad hoc lists, people will question every edge in the network. Useful, in my view, means trustable enough that coordinators won't dismiss it as anecdotal. Cleaned records from our institutional system solve most of that.
turns.utterance: That works for me. I do think people will trust it more if the collaborator suggestions come from cleaned publication records rather than an ad hoc compilation, even if the workshop format itself stays very simple.

turns.inner_thought: Five volunteers across disciplines would be ideal—small, consensual, and fast. We already have enough visible material from public profiles, ORCID pages, Scopus or Web of Science exports, and cluster CVs to mock up something credible for discussion. No need to trigger a larger governance conversation if this is just an exploratory pilot.
turns.utterance: In terms of scale, I wonder if we start with volunteers—say five researchers from different disciplines. For that, we could pull together the publication data we already have from public profiles and cluster CVs and see what kind of map emerges.

turns.inner_thought: Five is a reasonable subset. I hear 'publication data we already have' as the existing institutional records, which is ideal because then the structure can be reused later without rebuilding from scratch. If we ingest the subset properly now, we can keep the same architecture and just expand coverage later.
turns.utterance: Five researchers is fine for a pilot. If we use the existing institutional records, the network structure should be stable enough that we can reuse what we build later, even if the first round is intentionally small.

turns.inner_thought: I should keep emphasizing the non-evaluative framing. Team level is the protective phrase here; it signals that this is about collective patterns, not exposing individuals. If that lands, leadership can present it as developmental support rather than anything like ranking or oversight.
turns.utterance: Yes, and I think that concern about pressure is important. If we keep the first version at the team level, it should feel developmental rather than evaluative, which will matter a lot in how people receive it.

turns.inner_thought: No problem—the default can absolutely be team level. But facilitators will still need access to the underlying member connections or else they won't be able to act on what they see. That doesn't conflict with the framing; it's just necessary functionality behind the scenes.
turns.utterance: Agreed. The interface can open with team-level clusters, and then, when needed, facilitators can inspect the underlying member connections to understand what is driving a particular pattern.

turns.inner_thought: A second use case should make the value easy for steering to grasp. If the map reveals an unexpected adjacency between, say, public health and materials or economics and engineering, that's already enough to justify a workshop exercise. It doesn't need complete coverage of every publication type to be useful in that conversational sense.
turns.utterance: A second use case could be to highlight unexpected adjacency between fields. That would already be useful for finding potential collaborators, even if not every publication type is represented in the first pass.

turns.inner_thought: This is a good summary point. I'll package it in language that sounds aligned: lightweight pilot, existing publication data, team-level map, workshop scenarios. In my head, that still means a real pipeline, cleaned institutional records, drill-down capability, and signals sturdy enough to defend. If I present it that way, we can likely get approval and still preserve technical credibility.
turns.utterance: So, to summarize what we can take to the steering committee: we frame this as a lightweight pilot, built from existing publication data, centered on a team-level collaboration map, with a few workshop-style scenarios showing how it could help people spot potential collaborators without adding pressure. That feels like a good first package.
